teach.title: The thing something is done with

notice.ask: Which word in each sentence names the thing that is being used?

teach.say: When Latin names the tool — what somebody hits with, rides on, writes with — it uses **the ablative (the 'by/with' form)** and puts no preposition in front of it at all: *baculō verberat*, he beats with a stick. English needs the word *with*; Latin needs only the ending.

check.ask: Which word is the thing he is using?

teach.title: Tools in -us and -um end in -ō
teach.say: *Baculum* → *baculō*, *equus* → *equō*. It is the same -ō you have seen after *in* and *ex*; what is different here is that there is no little word in front of it. A bare -ō beside a verb of doing is usually the thing used.

show.say: baculō — the tool ends in -ō, with no preposition

teach.title: Tools in -a end in a long -ā
teach.say: *Lectīca* → *lectīcā*: the litter she is carried in. The macron carries the sense here too — *lectīca* would be the litter doing something, *lectīcā* is the litter being used. (*Viā longā ambulat* is the same ending doing a near neighbour's job: the road he goes by.)

teach.title: More than one thing: -īs
teach.say: Several things used take -īs, from either kind of word: *umerīs* on his shoulders, *verbīs* with words, *nummīs* with coins. Some of these are naturally plural — you carry a sack on two shoulders.

check.ask: Servus fessus saccum ___ portat. (umerus, more than one)

teach.title: *cum* is for company, never for a tool
teach.say: English says *with* for both, so this is the trap. A person who came along keeps *cum*: *cum servīs*. A thing that does the work has no *cum* at all: *equō vehitur*. If you can replace it with *and* — Julius and the slaves come — it is company; if it is what does the job, drop the *cum*.

check.ask: Is *umerīs* company or the thing used, and how do you know?

teach.title: Where it sits in the sentence
teach.say: The thing used need not wait for the verb: it can stand first. *Baculō Iūlius servum improbum verberat* — with a stick Julius beats the bad slave. Wherever it stands, what makes it the thing used is the bare ending with no *cum* in front.

check.ask: Which word says what the master accuses them with?

core.text: The tool or thing something is done with goes into **the ablative (the 'by/with' form)**, *ablātīvus īnstrūmentī*, with no preposition at all: *baculō verberat* = he beats with a stick; *equō vehitur* = he rides (is carried) on a horse; *oculīs videt* = he sees with his eyes. English needs *with* or *by*; Latin needs only the ending.
*With* has two jobs in English: the thing you use (*he cut it with a knife*) and the person you are alongside (*he sat with a friend*). Latin gives each its own grammar.
A thing used = plain ablative, no preposition. *Cum* + ablative is only for company (*cum amīcō*), never for tools.

invented.en: The shepherd hits the wolf with his stick.

core.text: English *by* covers both *struck by David* and *struck by a stone*; Latin does not. A person who does it takes *ā/ab* + ablative: *ā Dāvide*. A thing used takes the bare ablative: *lapide*. Test: if it could have done it on purpose, use *ab*; if it is a tool, leave the preposition out.

more.text: From the learner's notes: 'means' is how something gets done — grammarians split it into instrument, method and degree, the course treats them as one. English speakers reach for *cum* because it is the nearest word to *with*, but *cum* only ever means 'together with': *vir gladiō percutit* — he strikes with (using) the sword; *vir cum gladiō stat* — a man with (carrying) a sword stands there.

Ørberg cap. VI: *Lydia verbīs Mēdī dēlectātur* = *verba Mēdī Lydiam dēlectant*. The same plain ablative gives the price (*centum nummīs cōnstat* — costs a hundred coins, r08:59.1), the road travelled (*viā Latīnā*, r06:51.1) and, with an adjective, the manner (*magnā vōce clāmat* — shouts in a loud voice, r10:111.2). A&G §409 (means), §413 (accompaniment), §416 (price).
A few verbs take the bare ablative as a matter of course — *dēlectātur* is delighted by, *vehitur* is carried by — so beside those the bare -ō or -īs is nearly always the means.
